name: Staged-reaction steam turbogeneration
summary: Parsons's steam turbine spread the steam's expansion over many rows of blades on one fast-spinning shaft driving a generator, lighting an exhibition in 1887.
description: A steam turbine divides expansion among successive stationary and moving blade rows on a rotary shaft that drives an electrical generator. The scope includes operated machinery; an earlier Reynolds multistage reaction prototype preceded Parsons’s development.
tier_reason: A major reusable result, process or system within its field; broader multi-field or multi-generation dependence on this exact referent is not established.
why: Electric dynamos needed fast, smooth rotation that reciprocating steam engines delivered poorly.

market.note: The configuration can be supplied or used in economic production, independently of the date and scope of any first offer.

evidence.locator: “The Compound Steam Turbine”, opening, and fixed/moving blade paragraphs
evidence.supports: A February 1888 report states the preceding Newcastle exhibition’s lighting was provided by seventeen compound turbine motors, four spare, and describes successive steam expansion through blade stages.

evidence.locator: PDF p. 7 / printed p. 6, Parsons reaction and impulse turbine
evidence.supports: Explains successive stationary and rotating reaction blade rows, contrasting de Laval impulse machinery.

date.basis: The issue dated 18 February 1888 reports the Newcastle Exhibition lighting in “last year”.

events.statement: In 1887 the Newcastle Exhibition’s lighting was supplied by compound steam-turbine generators; the contemporary report counts seventeen motors including four spares.
events.scope: Parsons compound steam turbine driving an electric generator with steam expansion through successive blade stages.
applications: electric lighting at the Newcastle Exhibition
events.caveats: The 1888 report says seventeen units were supplied including four spares; it does not prove a sale, the exact exhibition operating interval, or the date of the Earl Percy installation. Reynolds had built a small staged reaction turbine about a decade earlier; neither 1884 nor this public use is claimed as the first concept.
